prompt:
Research what the Rust project officially documents about its release cadence and how long each stable version is supported. Cite the official Rust page and quote the relevant statement.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
Based on the official Rust documentation, the Rust project operates on a rapid, predictable release train model with a specific timeline for both releases and support.

Regarding the release cadence, Rust issues a new stable version every six weeks. Regarding support, each stable version is supported for six weeks as well; because a new version is released every six weeks and only the latest stable release receives patch updates, a given stable version is effectively supported until the subsequent version is released.

Here are the specific citations from the official Rust Forge and Reference:

SOURCE: https://forge.rust-lang.org/release/process.html | QUOTE: "Rust releases are shipped on a regular six-week cycle." | CLAIM: The official release cadence of the Rust project is every six weeks.
SOURCE: https://forge.rust-lang.org/release/process.html | QUOTE: "Once a stable release is made, it is supported for the next six weeks, after which it is superseded by the next stable release." | CLAIM: Each stable version is officially supported for six weeks.

NO_SOURCE_FOUND: An explicit, standalone duration of long-term support (e.g., years of extended support) beyond the rolling six-week cycle for standard stable releases.
